screens.title: Red Hat Ceph Storage: Block, Object, and File
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will explore how Red Hat Ceph Storage delivers three production-grade interfaces from one distributed cluster: block devices for VMs and containers, an S3-compatible object gateway, and a POSIX file system for shared access. I will define each interface, show concrete deployment and client commands you can run with cephadm, and highlight the operational choices architects must make—like placement groups, replication, load balancing, and metadata servers. You will see real command examples for creating an RBD image, deploying RGW instances and creating an S3 user, and creating CephFS with MDS daemons. I’ll also point out common mistakes, such as insufficient PGs, single replica pools for important data, and missing a load balancer for RGW clusters. By the end, you should be able to pick the right Ceph interface for a workload, run basic provisioning commands, and apply simple security precautions. Think about a database pod needing low-latency block devices and an application needing shared config files—we’ll map each to the correct Ceph interface and explain why.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to provision and operate each Ceph interface with confidence. First, you will configure and manage Ceph Block Devices to provide persistent, thin-provisioned disks for VMs and containers. That includes creating pools, initializing RBD, creating images, and mapping them to clients so they can be formatted and mounted. Second, you will deploy the Rados Gateway and provision S3 users, understanding how RGW exposes an S3-compatible A P I and why a load balancer and TLS are essential in production. Third, you will set up CephFS by deploying Metadata Servers and creating the metadata and data pools, and you will mount the filesystem with the kernel or FUSE client. Finally, you will compare performance characteristics and operational trade-offs—when to use RBD versus CephFS or object storage—and apply basic security measures using cephx and secure credentials. Each objective includes hands-on examples taken directly from cephadm and radosgw-admin commands so you can practice in a lab environment.

screens.title: Ceph Block Device (RBD): Definition and Purpose
screens.narratorSegment: Ceph Block Device, or RBD, provides virtual block devices backed by objects in Ceph pools. An RBD image behaves like a disk: you can create it, format it with a filesystem, attach it to a VM, or use it as a persistent volume for a container. The key property is thin provisioning: the image only consumes physical storage as data is written. RBD also supports snapshots and cloning, which are important for efficient backups and fast provisioning. A pool is required to host RBD images; the pool’s placement groups and replication policy determine distribution and durability. For example, creating an RBD image named my_vm_disk in rbd_pool and mapping it produces a device such as /dev/rbd0 on the client. A common misconception is that creating an image reserves full physical space; thin provisioning avoids that, but you must watch used capacity. Also, under-provisioned PGs or too few replicas will cause uneven distribution or risk data loss. Key takeaway: use RBD for workloads that need low-latency block semantics, like databases, and plan PGs and replicas for consistent performance and durability. How would you decide PG count for a growing cluster?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › RBD Definition
What is RBD?

RBD images are virtual block devices backed by objects in a Ceph pool. They support snapshots and cloning, and are thin-provisioned, making them efficient for VM disks and stateful containers.

Key properties
  • Thin provisioning: space used only when written
  • Snapshots and cloning for backups and fast provisioning
  • Requires proper PG and replica planning
Key Takeaway

Use RBD for low-latency block needs and ensure pools are sized and replicated for production durability.

Concrete example & command pattern
Create a pool, initialize for RBD, create an image, and map it to a client device.
# sudo cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create rbd_pool 128 128
# sudo cephadm shell -- rbd pool init rbd_pool
# sudo cephadm shell -- rbd create rbd_pool/my_vm_disk --size 100G
# sudo cephadm shell -- rbd ls rbd_pool
# On a client with rbd kernel module:
# sudo modprobe rbd
# sudo rbd map rbd_pool/my_vm_disk --id admin --keyring /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring
# Then format and mount the mapped block device as usual.
Common mistake
Using too few placement groups causes uneven distribution and hotspots.
Safety note
Use at least three replicas for production RBD pools to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Creating and Mapping an RBD Image — Step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating an RBD image and mapping it on a client. First, create or confirm a pool for RBD images, paying close attention to placement groups. Initialize the pool for RBD and create an image with the desired size. After creation, list images to verify. Mapping is a client-side operation that requires the rbd kernel module; the map command creates a block device representing the image. An important operational point: mapping should be done from the client host that will use the device or by the hypervisor passing the image to a guest. A concrete example is creating an image named app_disk_01 in my_rbd_pool and mapping it. Verify the mapped device exists, then format and mount it. A common misconception is that rbd map writes data immediately; it only exposes access—actual storage grows as you write because of thin provisioning. Finally, always validate capacity after provisioning and monitor PG distribution. Would the same pool be suitable for large numbers of small images or would you create separate pools by workload? Creating and Mapping an RBD Image — Step-by-step means create images in a pool, then map them from clients; thin provisioning means physical storage grows only as data is written.. In practical terms, commands and client mapping workflow with verification steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › RBD Workflow
Step-by-step commands
Follow these commands in a cephadm shell to create pools and an RBD image, then map on a client.
# Create a pool for RBD (example)
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create my_rbd_pool 64 64
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd pool init my_rbd_pool

# Create an RBD image named 'app_disk_01' with 50GB
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd create my_rbd_pool/app_disk_01 --size 50G

# Verify image exists
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd ls my_rbd_pool

# On the client host, ensure rbd module and map the image
sudo modprobe rbd
sudo rbd map my_rbd_pool/app_disk_01 --id admin --keyring /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring

# After mapping, format and mount the device as usual
# Example: sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/rbd0 && sudo mount /dev/rbd0 /mnt
Verify
Check rbd ls, mapped device presence, and filesystem integrity after mount.
Gotcha
Mapping requires client-side credentials and the rbd kernel module or a user-space mapping tool.
Concrete scenario

You provision a 50GB RBD for a PostgreSQL pod. Create the pool, create the image, map or provision through CSI to Kubernetes as a Persistent Volume, and ensure replication factor is at least 3. Monitor PG distribution so no single OSD carries disproportionate load.

Check your understanding
  1. Why thin provisioning matters for capacity planning?
  2. What credentials are needed on the client to map an image?
  3. When would you prefer a separate pool per workload?

screens.title: RBD vs CephFS vs RGW — Interface Selection
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right Ceph interface depends on how the application accesses data. RBD gives raw block devices and is best when an application needs direct block input and output, as in databases or virtual machines. CephFS provides a POSIX filesystem allowing many clients to mount a shared namespace simultaneously, which is ideal for shared configuration files, home directories, or applications requiring file semantics. RGW exposes an S3-compatible object A P I and is the correct choice for unstructured data, backups, media, and cloud-native apps using object storage. A common misconception is that CephFS always outperforms RBD for files; in many cases the kernel client for CephFS has good performance, but metadata-heavy workloads may need additional MDS capacity and tuning. Also, using RGW for file-like workloads can create awkward client-side complexity because objects are not POSIX. When designing architecture, ask: does the workload require POSIX semantics, low-latency block access, or object semantics with eventual consistency and bucket APIs? Each choice impacts pool design, replication, and operational practices. The takeaway: match semantics first, then tune replicas and PGs for performance. RBD vs CephFS vs RGW — Interface Selection means pick rbd for block, cephfs for shared posix files, and rgw for s3-style object storage; each has different operational trade-offs.. In practical terms, match access patterns to the correct ceph interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Interface Comparison
RBD
Block device, thin-provisioned, snapshots, ideal for VMs and databases.
Operational concerns: choose appropriate PG count, replica factor >= 3 for production, and map from clients with proper credentials.
CephFS
POSIX shared file system; requires MDS for metadata management.
Operational concerns: deploy enough MDS for metadata throughput, prefer kernel client for performance, and size metadata pools correctly.
RGW
S3-compatible object gateway for unstructured data and cloud-native apps.
Operational concerns: place RGW behind a load balancer, secure endpoints with TLS, and create S3 users with radosgw-admin.
Decision checklist
  • Does the workload require POSIX semantics? Use CephFS.
  • Does it need direct block I/O and low latency? Use RBD.
  • Is the data unstructured and accessed via HTTP/S3 APIs? Use RGW.

screens.title: Ceph Rados Gateway (RGW): Deploy and Create S3 Users
screens.narratorSegment: The Rados Gateway provides an S3- and Swift-compatible A P I in front of the RADOS object store. You deploy RGW as a service with cephadm and typically run at least two instances for availability. After deployment, you create S3 users using radosgw-admin and obtain an access key and a secret key for clients. These keys are then used by standard S3 tools and SDKs. In production you should place RGW instances behind a load balancer to provide a single endpoint, distribute traffic, and allow SSL termination. A common operational mistake is exposing RGW instances directly without a load balancer, which creates uneven traffic distribution and makes client failover complex. For security, always use HTTPS and strong user credentials, store keys securely, and implement network segmentation to limit RGW exposure. An example command sequence shows deploying two instances and creating a user with explicit keys, which you can then configure in s3cmd or an SDK for access validation. Consider how you would rotate keys and automate user lifecycle in your environment. Ceph Rados Gateway (RGW): Deploy and Create S3 Users means deploy rgw instances with cephadm, create s3 users with radosgw-admin, and front rgw with a load balancer and tls for production.. In practical terms, deploy rgw instances, create s3 credentials, and secure endpoints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › RGW Deployment
Deploy RGW with cephadm
Deploy one or more RGW instances for HA. Example command deploys two instances.
# Deploy an RGW instance named 'my-rgw' with two replicas
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply rgw my-rgw --placement="count=2"

# Verify RGW services
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph orch ls --service_type rgw

# Create an S3 user and return credentials
sudo cephadm shell -- radosgw-admin user create --uid=myuser --display-name="My User" --access-key=MYACCESSKEY --secret-key=MYSECRETKEY
# Save generated keys securely and configure client tools.
Pro tip
Automate user creation and key rotation with orchestration tooling to reduce manual exposure of keys.
Warning
Do not expose RGW instances directly in production without a load balancer and TLS.
Concrete example

After creating an S3 user, configure s3cmd or an SDK with the access and secret keys and try listing buckets. If using multiple RGW instances, point the client to a load-balanced endpoint to avoid manual failover logic.

Key Takeaway

RGW is scalable and fault tolerant when backed by multiple instances and a load balancer; secure access with TLS and strong credentials.

screens.title: RGW Client Access and Production Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Client access to RGW follows a clear flow: deploy RGW instances, create an S3 user, configure client credentials, and validate with a request such as listing buckets. For production, place a load balancer in front of RGW to provide a single stable endpoint and enable TLS termination. When creating a user with radosgw-admin, choose strong keys and store them in a secrets manager. A common mistake is using HTTP or weak keys in production, which exposes data and credentials. For testing, s3cmd is convenient: supply the endpoint, access key, and secret key to configure a profile and run a simple list or put operation. Consider how RGW scales: RGW is stateless regarding requests, so adding instances behind a load balancer increases throughput, while RADOS ensures object durability. For failover, ensure clients use the load balancer address and not individual instance addresses. A closing question: how will you implement key rotation and auditing for S3 users in a regulated environment? Testing with s3cmd: configure a profile using the access and secret keys, point to the load-balanced RGW endpoint, and run s3cmd ls to verify connectivity and permissions. For production, automate user lifecycle and key rotation, and keep logs for auditing.
Common mistake
Not using a load balancer; clients then require manual failover and can expose individual RGW addresses.
Pro tip
Use HTTPS and centralize certificates at the load balancer to simplify certificate management for RGW instances.

# Provide Access Key and Secret Key

screens.title: Ceph File System (CephFS): MDS and Metadata
screens.narratorSegment: CephFS is a POSIX-compliant distributed filesystem that allows multiple clients to mount the same namespace concurrently. It separates metadata from file data: Metadata Servers (MDS) manage directories, permissions, and namespace operations while the data itself resides in object pools on OSDs. This separation enables scalability for file data while centralizing metadata logic. Deploying CephFS requires creating both metadata and data pools and then deploying MDS daemons for high availability; two active MDS instances is a common configuration for redundancy. The kernel client typically delivers better performance than FUSE, but kernel compatibility and security policies determine the client choice. A common misconception is to assume CephFS handles metadata-heavy workloads without tuning; in high metadata rate scenarios you must provision more MDS capacity and ensure the metadata pool has sufficient PGs and replication. Key takeaway: choose CephFS when applications need POSIX semantics and shared mounts, and plan MDS capacity based on expected metadata operations. Ceph File System (CephFS): MDS and Metadata means mds handles namespace and metadata; data is stored on osds, so plan mds count and metadata pool sizing according to metadata workload.. In practical terms, posix-compliant shared filesystem with dedicated metadata servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › CephFS & MDS
How CephFS works

CephFS stores file data in RADOS pools while MDS daemons manage metadata — directories, inodes, and ACLs. This design separates fast path data I/O from metadata operations, enabling scale for different workload profiles.

Operational notes
  • Deploy multiple MDS daemons for availability and load sharing.
  • Metadata pool sizing and PGs matter for metadata-heavy workloads.
  • Prefer the kernel client when possible for best performance.
Key Takeaway

Use CephFS when applications require POSIX semantics and concurrent mounts; size MDS and metadata pools for expected metadata rates.

Commands to deploy CephFS
# Deploy MDS daemons (example: two instances)
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mds myfs --placement="count=2"

# Create pools needed for CephFS
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create myfs_metadata_pool 64 64
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create myfs_data_pool 128 128

# Create the filesystem
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph fs new myfs myfs_metadata_pool myfs_data_pool

# Verify status
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph fs ls
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph fs status myfs

screens.title: Mounting CephFS and Client Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Once CephFS is created and MDS daemons are active, clients can mount the filesystem using the kernel client or ceph-fuse. The kernel client typically offers better performance and lower C P U overhead, but it requires compatible kernel modules on the client host. The FUSE client is easier to deploy where kernel support is unavailable. To mount via kernel client, install ceph-common, create a mount point, and mount using the monitor addresses and admin credentials. Verify the mount by listing files and running small read and write tests. A common misconception is that mounting alone ensures performance; you must test metadata and data operations separately because the MDS can be the bottleneck for metadata-heavy workloads. If you expect many small file creates, consider increasing MDS capacity and metadata pool PGs. Key takeaway: validate mounts with real workload patterns and choose kernel client where feasible for production throughput. Mounting CephFS and Client Choices means kernel client for performance, fuse for portability; test with realistic file operations and tune mds for metadata workloads.. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › CephFS Mounts
Kernel client mount example
# On a client host
sudo dnf install -y ceph-common
sudo mkdir /mnt/cephfs
sudo mount -t ceph :6789,:6789:/ /mnt/cephfs -o name=admin,secretfile=/etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring
# Replace monitor addresses, use the admin keyring path on the client.
After mounting, test file and directory operations. For high rates of metadata ops, validate MDS failover and consider adding active MDS nodes.
FUSE client and performance notes

Use ceph-fuse when kernel modules are unavailable or when portability is required. Expect higher CPU overhead with FUSE and test performance against your expected workload. Measure both throughput and metadata operation latency to decide client and MDS sizing.

Check
Run file create/delete benchmarks and small-file tests to evaluate metadata performance.
Tip
Prefer kernel client for production where compatibility allows; tune MDS and metadata pool PGs for metadata-heavy apps.

screens.title: Authentication and Security: cephx, S3 Keys, and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Security is central to operating Ceph. Ceph uses cephx for internal authentication: clients present a username and secret key to access cluster resources. For RGW, S3 access and secret keys are the authentication mechanism for object APIs. Always use strong, unique credentials and store them in a secrets manager. Network segmentation should limit access to monitors, OSDs, MDS, and RGW to only authorized clients and administrative hosts. For RGW, use TLS to secure endpoints and terminate TLS at a load balancer if possible for centralized certificate management. A common misconception is that cephx alone is sufficient for public-facing endpoints; you still must encrypt in transit and use a load balancer to protect RGW instances. Also, rotate keys and audit access to detect misuse. For RBD and CephFS, client keys and keyrings control access—do not copy admin keys to client hosts in production. Key takeaway: apply least privilege, network segmentation, TLS, and key lifecycle policies to all Ceph interfaces. Authentication and Security: cephx, S3 Keys, and Best Practices means use cephx for ceph clients, s3 keys for rgw, secure endpoints with tls, and avoid distributing admin keys to clients.. In practical terms, secure access across rbd, rgw, and cephfs using keys, tls, and segmentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Lab Activity
Starter script (annotated)
# 1. Create pool and init for RBD
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create my_rbd_pool 64 64
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd pool init my_rbd_pool

# 2. Create RBD image
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd create my_rbd_pool/app_disk_01 --size 50G
sudo cephadm shell -- rbd ls my_rbd_pool

# 3. Deploy RGW if needed
sudo cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply rgw my-rgw-instance --placement="count=1"

# 4. Create S3 user and display keys
RGW_ACCESS_KEY=generated_access_key
RGW_SECRET_KEY=generated_secret_key
sudo cephadm shell -- radosgw-admin user create --uid=appuser --display-name="Application User" --access-key=${RGW_ACCESS_KEY} --secret-key=${RGW_SECRET_KEY}

# 5. (Optional) Test with s3cmd configured to use the new keys and RGW endpoint
# s3cmd ls
Instructor notes
  • Run pool and image creation inside cephadm shell to ensure access to cluster keys.
  • Map RBD images only on hosts that will use them and keep client keys limited.
  • Store S3 keys in a secrets manager and avoid exposing them in plain logs.

This activity exercises provisioning and validation steps for RBD and RGW and highlights security and operational checks required for production readiness.

Keep these ideas in mind when designing storage for VMs, containers, and shared-file applications so you match interface semantics, plan for scale, and protect access. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will explore how Red Hat Ceph Storage delivers three production-grade interfaces from one distributed cluster: block devices for VMs and containers, an S3-compatible object gateway, and a POSIX file system for shared access. I will define each interface, show concrete deployment and client commands you can run with cephadm, and highlight the operational choices architects must make—like placement groups, replication, load balancing, and metadata servers. You will see real command examples for creating an RBD image, deploying RGW instances and creating an S3 user, and creating CephFS with MDS daemons. I’ll also point out common mistakes, such as insufficient PGs, single replica pools for important data, and missing a load balancer for RGW clusters. By the end, you should be able to pick the right Ceph interface for a workload, run basic provisioning commands, and apply simple security precautions. Think about a database pod needing low-latency block devices and an application needing shared config files—we’ll map each to the correct Ceph interface and explain why.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to provision and operate each Ceph interface with confidence. First, you will configure and manage Ceph Block Devices to provide persistent, thin-provisioned disks for VMs and containers. That includes creating pools, initializing RBD, creating images, and mapping them to clients so they can be formatted and mounted. Second, you will deploy the Rados Gateway and provision S3 users, understanding how RGW exposes an S3-compatible A P I and why a load balancer and TLS are essential in production. Third, you will set up CephFS by deploying Metadata Servers and creating the metadata and data pools, and you will mount the filesystem with the kernel or FUSE client. Finally, you will compare performance characteristics and operational trade-offs—when to use RBD versus CephFS or object storage—and apply basic security measures using cephx and secure credentials. Each objective includes hands-on examples taken directly from cephadm and radosgw-admin commands so you can practice in a lab environment.

This checklist converts objectives into practised tasks. Practice creating an RBD pool with recommended placement groups, initialize it for RBD use, and create an RBD image which you can then list and map on a client. For RGW, practice deploying one or more gateway instances, create an S3 user and retrieve keys, and run a simple client command to list buckets. For CephFS, deploy two MDS daemons for high availability and create both metadata and data pools before creating the filesystem. As you perform these tasks, test common failure modes: confirm data distribution across OSDs, validate RGW behind a load balancer, and check MDS failover. Each task reinforces a core skill: provisioning, client access, and operational validation. In the lab activity at the end of the chapter you'll combine steps by creating an RBD image and an S3 user on an existing cluster, and optionally test S3 access with s3cmd. Treat this checklist as the minimum rehearsal to reach competency.

Ceph Block Device, or RBD, provides virtual block devices backed by objects in Ceph pools. An RBD image behaves like a disk: you can create it, format it with a filesystem, attach it to a VM, or use it as a persistent volume for a container. The key property is thin provisioning: the image only consumes physical storage as data is written. RBD also supports snapshots and cloning, which are important for efficient backups and fast provisioning. A pool is required to host RBD images; the pool’s placement groups and replication policy determine distribution and durability. For example, creating an RBD image named my_vm_disk in rbd_pool and mapping it produces a device such as /dev/rbd0 on the client. A common misconception is that creating an image reserves full physical space; thin provisioning avoids that, but you must watch used capacity. Also, under-provisioned PGs or too few replicas will cause uneven distribution or risk data loss. Key takeaway: use RBD for workloads that need low-latency block semantics, like databases, and plan PGs and replicas for consistent performance and durability. How would you decide PG count for a growing cluster?

Let's walk through creating an RBD image and mapping it on a client. First, create or confirm a pool for RBD images, paying close attention to placement groups. Initialize the pool for RBD and create an image with the desired size. After creation, list images to verify. Mapping is a client-side operation that requires the rbd kernel module; the map command creates a block device representing the image. An important operational point: mapping should be done from the client host that will use the device or by the hypervisor passing the image to a guest. A concrete example is creating an image named app_disk_01 in my_rbd_pool and mapping it. Verify the mapped device exists, then format and mount it. A common misconception is that rbd map writes data immediately; it only exposes access—actual storage grows as you write because of thin provisioning. Finally, always validate capacity after provisioning and monitor PG distribution. Would the same pool be suitable for large numbers of small images or would you create separate pools by workload? Creating and Mapping an RBD Image — Step-by-step means create images in a pool, then map them from clients; thin provisioning means physical storage grows only as data is written.. In practical terms, commands and client mapping workflow with verification steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right Ceph interface depends on how the application accesses data. RBD gives raw block devices and is best when an application needs direct block input and output, as in databases or virtual machines. CephFS provides a POSIX filesystem allowing many clients to mount a shared namespace simultaneously, which is ideal for shared configuration files, home directories, or applications requiring file semantics. RGW exposes an S3-compatible object A P I and is the correct choice for unstructured data, backups, media, and cloud-native apps using object storage. A common misconception is that CephFS always outperforms RBD for files; in many cases the kernel client for CephFS has good performance, but metadata-heavy workloads may need additional MDS capacity and tuning. Also, using RGW for file-like workloads can create awkward client-side complexity because objects are not POSIX. When designing architecture, ask: does the workload require POSIX semantics, low-latency block access, or object semantics with eventual consistency and bucket APIs? Each choice impacts pool design, replication, and operational practices. The takeaway: match semantics first, then tune replicas and PGs for performance. RBD vs CephFS vs RGW — Interface Selection means pick rbd for block, cephfs for shared posix files, and rgw for s3-style object storage; each has different operational trade-offs.. In practical terms, match access patterns to the correct ceph interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Rados Gateway provides an S3- and Swift-compatible A P I in front of the RADOS object store. You deploy RGW as a service with cephadm and typically run at least two instances for availability. After deployment, you create S3 users using radosgw-admin and obtain an access key and a secret key for clients. These keys are then used by standard S3 tools and SDKs. In production you should place RGW instances behind a load balancer to provide a single endpoint, distribute traffic, and allow SSL termination. A common operational mistake is exposing RGW instances directly without a load balancer, which creates uneven traffic distribution and makes client failover complex. For security, always use HTTPS and strong user credentials, store keys securely, and implement network segmentation to limit RGW exposure. An example command sequence shows deploying two instances and creating a user with explicit keys, which you can then configure in s3cmd or an SDK for access validation. Consider how you would rotate keys and automate user lifecycle in your environment. Ceph Rados Gateway (RGW): Deploy and Create S3 Users means deploy rgw instances with cephadm, create s3 users with radosgw-admin, and front rgw with a load balancer and tls for production.. In practical terms, deploy rgw instances, create s3 credentials, and secure endpoints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Client access to RGW follows a clear flow: deploy RGW instances, create an S3 user, configure client credentials, and validate with a request such as listing buckets. For production, place a load balancer in front of RGW to provide a single stable endpoint and enable TLS termination. When creating a user with radosgw-admin, choose strong keys and store them in a secrets manager. A common mistake is using HTTP or weak keys in production, which exposes data and credentials. CephFS is a POSIX-compliant distributed filesystem that allows multiple clients to mount the same namespace concurrently. It separates metadata from file data: Metadata Servers (MDS) manage directories, permissions, and namespace operations while the data itself resides in object pools on OSDs. This separation enables scalability for file data while centralizing metadata logic. Deploying CephFS requires creating both metadata and data pools and then deploying MDS daemons for high availability; two active MDS instances is a common configuration for redundancy. The kernel client typically delivers better performance than FUSE, but kernel compatibility and security policies determine the client choice. A common misconception is to assume CephFS handles metadata-heavy workloads without tuning; in high metadata rate scenarios you must provision more MDS capacity and ensure the metadata pool has sufficient PGs and replication. Key takeaway: choose CephFS when applications need POSIX semantics and shared mounts, and plan MDS capacity based on expected metadata operations. Security is central to operating Ceph. Ceph uses cephx for internal authentication: clients present a username and secret key to access cluster resources. For RGW, S3 access and secret keys are the authentication mechanism for object APIs. Always use strong, unique credentials and store them in a secrets manager. Network segmentation should limit access to monitors, OSDs, MDS, and RGW to only authorized clients and administrative hosts. For RGW, use TLS to secure endpoints and terminate TLS at a load balancer if possible for centralized certificate management. A common misconception is that cephx alone is sufficient for public-facing endpoints; you still must encrypt in transit and use a load balancer to protect RGW instances. Let's summarize the three essential concepts you should remember. First, Ceph exposes three distinct interfaces—RBD for block, RGW for object, and CephFS for POSIX file access—and each fits specific workload semantics. Second, operational settings like placement groups and replica count affect performance and durability; always size PGs appropriately and use at least three replicas in production for critical data. Third, security matters: use cephx for client authentication, issue S3 keys through radosgw-admin, front RGW with a load balancer, and secure all endpoints with TLS.
